The zebra (Diplodus hottentotus) is a coastal sparid that attains a moderate maximum body size, with the ultimate total length recorded at 60 centimeters [Li = 60 centimeters]. This asymptotic length is comparable to that of other Diplodus species inhabiting the same temperate reef systems, placing the species among the larger members of its genus. Young-of-year individuals first become apparent in the ichthyoplankton during the late spring, following a brief incubation period. At a stable water temperature of 25.9 °C [T = 25.9 °C], hatching occurs after an age at birth of only 4 days [ab = 4 days], a rapid developmental pace that is characteristic of many sparid fishes with pelagic eggs. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva is minute, weighing a mere 0.00032 grams [Wwb = 0.00032 grams] upon chorion rupture, a mass that reflects the small egg diameter typical of broadcast-spawning teleosts. This lecithotrophic larva must progress through yolk absorption and the onset of exogenous feeding within a narrow window before the ontogenetic point of no return is reached.

As the larvae grow and undergo metamorphosis, the juvenile recruits gradually take on the adult body plan and shift to a benthic existence. Field surveys indicate that the total length at puberty is reached at 28 centimeters [Lp = 28 centimeters], a measurement that serves as a key demographic threshold marking the transition to the immature post-metamorphic stage capable of gametogenesis. The corresponding wet weight at puberty is 345 grams [Wwp = 345 grams], derived from the length-weight relationship established for this population. This size at maturity is somewhat smaller than that reported for the closely related Diplodus sargus, potentially reflecting differences in the local thermal regime or food availability. Once a fish surpasses this length, gonadal recrudescence becomes possible, and the individual enters the pool of reproductively viable organisms that will contribute to the annual spawning aggregation. The onset of first reproduction typically occurs not long after the fish reaches this critical size, although some delay may be imposed by the need to acquire sufficient lipid reserves.

Reproductive adults exhibited a gonadosomatic index (GSI) of 5.5% [GSI = 5.5%] when sampled during the peak spawning season at the local ambient temperature of 25.9 °C [T = 25.9 °C]. Gravid individuals are commonly encountered on shallow rocky reefs during the summer months, with the spawning event itself involving the synchronized release of gametes into the water column. The fertilized ovum is transparent and buoyant, drifting as ichthyoplankton until the onset of embryonic development is complete and the yolk-dependent embryo is ready to hatch.

The ultimate wet weight attained by this species reaches 3557 grams [Wwi = 3557 grams], representing the maximum recorded adult body mass in the wild. This substantial mass, which corresponds to the largest individuals in the population, is typically observed only in older, slow-growing fish that have accumulated considerable somatic tissue over many years. The species is relatively long-lived for a sparid of its size; maximum recorded longevity extends to approximately 12,045 days [am = approximately 12,045 days] when measured at the species' typical thermal regime of 25.9 °C [T = 25.9 °C]. This extended lifespan allows for multiple reproductive seasons and a high degree of iteroparity, which buffers the population against occasional years of poor recruitment. Older individuals often occupy the most productive territories on the reef and likely contribute disproportionately to the annual reproductive output of the population through their larger body size and higher fecundity. Senescence in this species has not been well documented, but field observations suggest a gradual decline in body condition among the oldest individuals.

Comparisons with other members of the genus reveal that Diplodus hottentotus occupies an intermediate position along the life-history continuum. The gonadosomatic index of 5.5% [GSI = 5.5%] was recorded at 25.9 °C [T = 25.9 °C], while the ultimate total length of 60 centimeters [Li = 60 centimeters] exceeds that of many closely related species found in the Mediterranean basin. The age at birth of 4 days [ab = 4 days] at 25.9 °C [T = 25.9 °C] is brief relative to species that produce demersal or adhesive eggs, but consistent with the rapid embryogenesis of pelagic spawners. The wet weight at birth of 0.00032 grams [Wwb = 0.00032 grams] places the newly hatched larva among the smallest of the diplodine sparids, although larvae grow quickly after the initiation of exogenous feeding. Longevity estimates of approximately 12,045 days [am = approximately 12,045 days] at 25.9 °C [T = 25.9 °C] suggest that this species is slower to reach senescence than its tropical counterparts, likely due to the moderating influence of the temperate waters it inhabits.
